papers.title: Metal Additive Manufacturing of Engineering Alloys: Process–Material Interactions, Defect Formation, Property Optimization and a Decision-Making Framework
papers.abstract: Metal additive manufacturing (MAM) has evolved into a strategic manufacturing route for producing, repairing, and remanufacturing high-value components; however, process selection and optimization remain challenging because manufacturing conditions, alloy behaviour, defect formation, microstructural evolution, and final properties are strongly interdependent. This review provides a critical and comparative assessment of four representative MAM technologies—Laser Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF), Laser Metal Deposition (LMD), a laser-based variant of Directed Energy Deposition (DED), Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM), and Metal Binder Jetting (MBJ)—with particular emphasis on their interactions with titanium alloys, nickel-based superalloys, steels, and aluminium alloys. Rather than comparing these technologies solely in terms of productivity, cost, or geometrical capability, the review examines the physical and metallurgical mechanisms governing thermal history, solidification or densification, phase evolution, defect formation, microstructure, and resulting component performance. Particular attention is given to porosity, lack of fusion, cracking, residual stresses, distortion, anisotropy, and surface integrity, together with process-specific mitigation and post-processing strategies. Based on the relationships identified across the literature, an integrated Process–Material–Defect–Property (PMDP) framework is proposed to connect manufacturing conditions and alloy-specific responses with defect and microstructural evolution, resulting properties, and in-service performance. A complementary PMDP-based decision pathway is introduced to support performance-driven alloy–process selection, risk identification, thermal and parameter optimization, post-processing definition, and final performance validation. The analysis demonstrates that no universally optimal MAM technology exists; instead, process suitability depends on the compatibility between material behaviour, manufacturing physics, component requirements, and the targeted material state. Future progress is expected to rely on transferable process–material maps, additive manufacturing (AM)-specific alloy design, mechanism-informed in-situ monitoring, physics-informed data-driven modelling, and adaptive closed-loop control. The proposed framework therefore provides a structured pathway towards material- and performance-driven, state-controlled, and ultimately performance-certified metal additive manufacturing.

papers.title: Review on Bio-HEA-based orthopedic implants: Stress shielding, elastic modulus, and the role of mathematical modeling.
papers.abstract: BackgroundBio-inspired high-entropy alloys (Bio-HEAs) are emerging as materials for orthopedic implants because of their high strength, corrosion resistance, compositional flexibility, and biocompatibility. Their tunable mechanical properties may reduce elastic mismatch with bone and mitigate stress shielding and implant loosening.ObjectiveThis review evaluates Bio-HEAs for orthopedic applications, emphasizing elastic modulus tailoring, stress-shielding mitigation, microstructural control, biological response, and mathematical modeling.MethodsLiterature on Bio-HEAs for biomedical applications was reviewed, focusing on composition-structure-property relationships, elastic modulus, phase stability, biological response, and computational approaches. Experimental findings were considered alongside molecular dynamics (MD), continuum elasticity, partial differential equation (PDE)-based approaches, and finite element method (FEM) simulations.ResultsReported Bio-HEAs exhibit elastic moduli ranging approximately from 10 to 30 GPa, providing opportunities to reduce mechanical mismatch with cortical bone. Atomic size mismatch, lattice distortion, phase constitution, and microstructural features influence elastic behavior. MD, continuum models, and FEM provide complementary insights across length scales, while integrated multiscale approaches can improve implant-level predictions and support patient-specific design.ConclusionBio-HEAs offer potential for mechanically compatible orthopedic implants. Integrating materials design with multiscale mathematical modeling may enable improved control of elastic behavior, stress distribution, and implant performance, although experimental validation and clinically relevant modeling are required.

papers.title: PolicyIK: High-Precision Inverse Kinematics for Robot Arms with Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Inverse kinematics (IK) converts end-effector pose commands into joint motion, and many vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely on it to act on a given arm and to transfer across embodiments. Precise IK remains laborious: redundancy and singularities complicate the inverse mapping, execution depends on hand-tuned controllers, and training data on physical robots are costly to collect. We present PolicyIK, a goal-conditioned reinforcement learning policy for high-precision IK. It updates joint-position references from pose feedback and observes its accumulated reference relative to the measured joints, so it can retain the offset that the position controller needs at rest. Two-scale pose errors with an error-dependent action gain resolve millimeter residuals while preserving large motions. Progress and dwell rewards teach it to both reach the tolerance and stay within it. In simulation, a single attempt by the trained PPO policy keeps the mean errors over the final second within 1 mm and 0.2° on 93.5% of held-out tasks, and a deployment protocol raises success to 98.9%. When trained directly on a physical arm with an off-policy RL learner, PolicyIK achieves higher reaching and holding success than all four classical IK controllers under the same time budgets. In simulated pick-and-place, PolicyIK executes the end-effector commands of the $π_{0.5}$ VLA policy with 95.7% success. These results show that reinforcement learning can provide high-precision inverse kinematics for robot arms. Code is available at https://github.com/Tinaliu0123/PolicyIK.

papers.title: Conformal Prediction at Performative Equilibrium: The Price of Performativity
papers.abstract: Conformal prediction gives finite-sample coverage when calibration and test points are exchangeable, but exchangeability can fail when deployment changes the data distribution. We study conformal prediction in performative settings, where the deployed predictor affects the data distribution, and seek prediction sets valid at performative equilibrium: coverage must hold under $D(f^\star)$ for a performatively stable predictor $f^\star$. Under total-variation $L$-sensitivity of the distribution map, we prove a phase transition at $L=1$. If $L \ge 1$, no finite-sample procedure can uniformly guarantee both equilibrium-valid coverage and nontrivial prediction sets. If $L<1$, the minimax excess miscoverage over informative procedures is $\widetildeΩ(1/((1-L)\sqrt{n}))$, implying a sample-complexity inflation of order $1/(1-L)^2$ for fixed excess miscoverage. Our main technical tool is a transfer theorem: any procedure returning a predictor within $\varepsilon$ of equilibrium yields equilibrium-valid coverage up to an additive $L\varepsilon$ term after split-conformal calibration. We instantiate the theorem with two retraining algorithms: a model-free method for discretizable classes and a parametric tail-averaged method that matches the $n$- and $L$-dependence of this rate up to logarithmic factors. Experiments, including semi-synthetic credit scoring, demonstrate the predicted threshold behavior and scaling laws.

papers.title: De Rham cohomological architectures for PINNs and PDEs with topological holes
papers.abstract: We attempt to alleviate failure modes of classical physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in scenarios of topological pathologies corresponding to punctures, holes, poles, and voids by introducing de Rham cohomological augmentations, or Hodge-de Rham PINNs. Vanilla PINNs often encounter pitfalls in hole-based settings due to discontinuous interfaces, nonzero closed path integration, path dependence, correspondence to exact forms via the exterior derivative, etc., therefore we absolve traditional failures via parameterizing a 1-form by the Hodge-Morrey-Friedrichs (HMF) decomposition for manifolds with boundary, drawing a connection to de Rham cohomology such as through the HMF isomorphism theorem. 1-forms can act as representations of scalar-valued PDE solutions through integral operator mappings. We propose performing a PINN-based loss on the parameterized 1-form through an associated PDE, which subsequently solves the potential-based PINN problem and moreover remedies the failures of vanilla PINNs via the Sobolev-regular operator under a Fréchet differentiation interconnection. The operator relationship often has a nontrivial closed-form and often requires integration or a case-by-case analysis, which we address thoroughly in our experiments. When an integrability condition is not met on our losses, we can equip exhaustion functions to train the networks. We demonstrate our methods on the Aharonov-Bohm effect, which, to our understanding, is largely nonexistent in PINN literature. We develop theoretical guarantees of our methods and demonstrate our pathological safeguards on a broad selection of topologically-adverse problems, including scenarios of inexact forms, and those of nontrivial harmonics and coexact terms.

papers.title: NovoCRF: Globally Normalized De Novo Peptide Sequencing on a Prefix-Mass Lattice
papers.abstract: De novo peptide sequencing has moved from dynamic programming over hand-designed or generative scores to large transformers that learn the task end to end. We present NovoCRF, a conditional random field (CRF) whose states are prefix masses, so that its paths are exactly the peptides within +/-0.06 Da of the precursor mass. A small network scores each edge from physics-derived ion-match features and is trained with its scores globally normalized over all mass-feasible peptides. To our knowledge, NovoCRF is the first de novo method trained with exact normalization over all mass-feasible peptides. Our software has three modules, each with exactly one job: a precursor mass finder recovers the accurate precursor mass from MS1, the CRF finds the peptides that fit the precursor mass by exact k-best decoding, and two BiGRU rerankers add sequence context and internal-fragment evidence. The model has 310k parameters and trains in about 17 GPU-hours. On seven held-out data-dependent acquisition datasets published in 2026 (126,262 labeled spectra), NovoCRF's mean peptide recall is 42.4%, against 39.1% for Casanovo v5 with five beams, and its amino-acid recall 64.0% against 53.1%, at 1,746 spectra/s on 18 CPU threads, 55x Casanovo's throughput on a GPU. Split by fragment evidence, NovoCRF leads on labels with up to three peptide bonds without a b or y ion, and Casanovo only beyond. NovoCRF can also search modifications it was never trained on at their exact mass: it finds 32.1% of the hydroxyproline peptides of a lion bone sample.

papers.title: Post-stratified importance sampling
papers.abstract: Importance sampling is a building block of modern statistical computing, but the weighted estimate is prone to high or infinite variance. Moreover, its empirical standard error is often unreliable, leaving importance sampling without practical uncertainty quantification. Motivated by multilevel regression and poststratification (MRP) in survey sampling, we propose post-stratified importance sampling (PIS) for estimating target expectations from proposal draws. PIS reformulates arbitrarily high-dimensional weighting into two one-dimensional probabilistic modeling problems: regression for the conditional mean given the importance ratio and marginal density estimation for the importance ratio. Different modeling choices yield a family of PIS estimators, encompassing ordinary importance sampling as a special case. We develop a model-based implementation that combines one-dimensional Gaussian process regression for the conditional mean and score-informed heavy-tailed density estimation for the marginal law, using both the observed weights and the available density evaluations. We study the oracle gains of PIS and establish consistency under general and model-specific conditions. Simulations and applications to cross-validation demonstrate improvements in estimation accuracy and uncertainty quantification.

papers.title: AgentAM: An AI Agent for Spatter- and Defect-Aware Process Optimization in Laser Powder Bed Fusion
papers.abstract: Predictive models for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) are rarely used on the shop floor because querying them requires programming and model-specific knowledge. We present AgentAM, a large language model (LLM) agent that gives process engineers natural-language access to CFD-trained surrogates of spatter and melt pool geometry for SS316L through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Polynomial surrogates trained on 279 single-track simulations predict melt pool dimensions ($R^2 \geq 0.95$) and spatter volume ($R^2 = 0.83$ on test data) at any power-velocity point in the trained range, and geometric criteria assign each point a geometry-derived defect regime (keyhole, lack of fusion, balling or stable) that matches the regime obtained from the simulated geometry in 93.4% of tracks under cross-validation. The agent selects and parameterizes tools for prediction, process-window scans and constrained optimization. Minimum-spatter optima often sat within 10 $μ$m of the lack-of-fusion boundary; a margin-aware optimizer moved them away from all thresholds and raised the estimated probability of remaining classified Good from 0.94 to 1.00 under an assumed 2% process drift, and from 0.72 to 0.91 when jointly sampled cross-validated geometry residuals were added. About 40-50 well-spread simulations sufficed to reproduce the defect map. To evaluate the agent layer, we introduce a 145-prompt benchmark scored against direct tool calls, plus eight prompts (40 runs) on margin-aware requests. Over the 725 runs of the main benchmark the agent passed the intended inputs in 98.5% of parsing prompts, reported the scored spatter values and defect classes faithfully and met every stated constraint in the 65 feasible optimization runs, within a median 1.0% of the brute-force optimum.

papers.title: Macrocanonical Generator Networks: Data-Efficient Neural Surrogates for Amortized Physics Simulation
papers.abstract: Many scientific simulations are computationally expensive, limiting their use in simulation-based inference, uncertainty quantification, and decision making. We introduce macrocanonical generator networks, a framework for learning fast, data-efficient neural surrogates for amortized simulation of stationary physical processes by matching multiscale statistics of a target process. Inspired by microcanonical maximum-entropy synthesis, which matches feature statistics per sample by inner-loop optimization, our approach instead trains a neural generator to satisfy the same constraints in expectation, preserving physically realistic sample-to-sample fluctuations. We prove that gradient-descent training induces preconditioned gradient-descent dynamics in sample space that inherit the symmetry-preservation properties of the microcanonical gradient descent of Bruna and Mallat, amortizing its per-sample inner-loop optimization into a single training run after which every sample is generated in one forward pass. We further show that residual generator parameterizations initialized near the identity, trained with a small learning rate, preserve entropy locally during early optimization and mitigate mode collapse. Experiments on cosmology and fluid simulations show that macrocanonical generators recover realistic samples from extremely small training sets, in some cases a single training example, while generating new realizations more than $10^6$ times faster per sample than the reference simulator and more than $10^3$ times faster than microcanonical gradient descent. The trained generators can be reused for downstream pretraining, including simulation-based inference, providing a data-efficient route to multi-fidelity scientific machine learning workflows.

papers.title: Solving the Nonlinear Westervelt Equation in Ultrasound Propagation Using Physics-Informed Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Modeling the nonlinear acoustic wave propagation in biological tissues needs accuracy, especially in ultrasound imaging and therapeutic applications. The 1D Westervelt equation, \( p_{xx} - p_{tt} + γ\, p_{ttt} + η\,(p^{2})_{tt}=0, \) could be used to describe a finite-amplitude ultrasound propagation in these tissues. This equation accounts for nonlinearity, \(η\), and attenuation, \(γ\). To solve this equation, we observe that traditional solvers may struggle to do so correctly. This is due to the difficulties arising from the nonlinear nature of the equation. We solve the equation by defining three synthetic cases - linear (\(η=0.001\), \(γ=10^{-6}\)), shock-dominated (\(η=0.02\), \(γ=10^{-6}\)), and dissipation-dominated (\(η=0.01\), \(γ=5\times10^{-4}\)) - and using Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to showcase the solution. A sinusoidal activation function is used to capture the oscillatory behavior of the problem. The results of our study, with PDE residual converging to at least \(10^{-6}\), boundary condition loss to \(10^{-5}\), and the PINN loss converging to \(10^{-5}\) for each case at \(30,000\) epochs, show that \(γ\) scales the rate of amplitude decay, while \(η\) governs frequency-dependent phase speeds.

summary_zh.validation: 在三个合成数值算例上以损失收敛性进行验证。

summary_en.result: Residuals converge to roughly 10^-6, and the attenuation and nonlinearity coefficients are shown to govern amplitude decay and frequency-dependent phase speed, respectively.
summary_en.validation: Validation relies on loss convergence across three synthetic numerical cases without experimental or benchmark comparison.

papers.title: Distributed Linear Bandits for Freshness-Aware Preprocessing in MEC-Enabled Digital Twin Networks
papers.abstract: Digital twins (DTs) require timely updates from Internet of Things (IoT) devices to accurately represent the state of the corresponding physical systems, but transmitting large data volumes can compromise freshness. Moreover, different task classes have distinct computational demands and freshness requirements, while stochastic task generation and sizes complicate resource allocation. In this paper, we propose a freshness-aware framework in which multi-access edge computing (MEC) servers preprocess IoT data, reducing transmission volume and DT-server processing load. The framework establishes mutual support between DT and MEC servers. The DTs determine feasible CPU-allocation strategies guaranteeing class-specific age-of-information (AoI) requirements under specified workload, delay, and update-generation bounds. MEC servers collaboratively identify the feasible strategy minimizing expected freshness-normalized preprocessing delay. We formulate CPU-strategy selection as a fixed-confidence distributed best-arm identification problem in linear bandits, with MEC servers as agents and CPU allocations across task classes as arms. We employ DistLinGapE, a distributed collaborative learning method, to coordinate exploration and share observations. Numerical results show that the method identifies the optimal feasible strategy and reduces preprocessing delay when deployed under stationary task-class assignments and workload statistics. Collaboration yields an identification speedup nearly proportional to the number of participating MEC servers in the evaluated settings.

papers.title: Enabling risk and reliability analysis in next-generation computational tools via multifidelity methods
papers.abstract: Risk and reliability analysis are fundamental to the design, assessment, and operation of safety-critical complex systems; however, their integration into next-generation computational tools is constrained by the cost of uncertainty quantification with expensive computational models. The computational challenge is particularly prohibitive for tail-sensitive quantities, such as probabilities of failure, conditional values-at-risk, and buffered probabilities of failure, where accurate estimation can require a large number of model evaluations. Multifidelity methods provide a framework for addressing this computational bottleneck by combining information from models of varying accuracy and cost while retaining the predictive accuracy of the high-fidelity model. This review summarizes the state of the art in methods that enable scalable risk and reliability analysis using multifidelity control variates, multifidelity importance sampling, and multifidelity active learning.

papers.title: CRONOS: Benchmarking Non-Episodic Reinforcement Learning for Robotic Manipulation
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is promising for adapting robot policies to unstructured real-world environments. However, standard RL pipelines rely on episodic training with frequent scene resets, which is impractical for real-world deployment due to the need for substantial human intervention. While prior work has studied non-episodic RL in relatively small policies trained from scratch, its behavior when fine-tuning modern large-scale pre-trained vision-language-action (VLA) models remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce CRONOS, a simulation benchmark for RL fine-tuning of VLAs under non-episodic scene resets. CRONOS leverages high-fidelity physics simulators and adopts shared-scene multi-task settings. Using CRONOS, we show that naively fine-tuning pre-trained policies fails in non-episodic settings due to shifts in object configurations and end-effector poses; however, these challenges can be mitigated through targeted reset allocation and by addressing biases in pre-trained models. Moreover, we find that non-episodic training enhances long-horizon manipulation and improves generalization to previously unseen object configurations and task sequences. Project page: https://embodiedai-ntu.github.io/cronos/

papers.title: Trajectory Evaluation via Rollout-Free World Model for End-to-end Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Although existing candidate trajectory evaluators have substantially improved end-to-end planning accuracy, their underlying mechanism remains suboptimal. Model-based evaluators typically make scoring future-aware by explicitly predicting candidate-conditioned future states over the planning horizon, which we term rollout. However, rollout incurs high inference cost and accumulates prediction errors. We argue that planning does not require reconstructing a full future scene for each candidate, but only future-relevant information for reliable comparison. We therefore propose RFWorld, a Rollout-Free World model for end-to-end trajectory evaluation. RFWorld constructs a shared scene memory and shapes it into a future-readable representation via lightweight training-time temporal readout with semantic supervision, keeping training overhead low. At inference time, candidate trajectories directly query the shared memory via sparse spatial readout for scoring, reducing computation by roughly the planning horizon times the number of candidate trajectories, while avoiding recursive rollout errors. Experiments on NAVSIM and Bench2Drive show that RFWorld learns a more planning-aligned world representation and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

summary_zh.method: 构建共享场景记忆并用轻量时序读出替代逐候选rollout。
summary_zh.result: 在NAVSIM和Bench2Drive上达到SOTA并大幅降低推理计算。
summary_zh.validation: 在自动驾驶基准数据集上进行仿真评测。

summary_en.method: The authors propose a rollout-free world model that builds a shared scene memory and lets candidate trajectories query it via sparse spatial readout for scoring.
summary_en.result: The approach achieves state-of-the-art planning performance on NAVSIM and Bench2Drive while cutting inference computation substantially.
summary_en.validation: Evaluated on the NAVSIM and Bench2Drive autonomous driving simulation benchmarks.

papers.title: Deep Neural Operator Learning for stochastic heat equations and applications
papers.abstract: In this paper, we establish a universal approximation theorem for solution operators of semilinear stochastic heat equations in spatial dimension \(d\ge2\), extending deep neural operator approximation results to SPDEs with distribution-valued Gaussian forcing. A smooth Fourier cutoff reduces the forcing to finitely many measurements, while Besov and Schauder estimates control the resulting solution error. The finite-dimensional solution map is then approximated by ReLU branch networks together with grid-based trunk functions, yielding explicit bounds on the numbers of forcing measurements and trunk functions and approximation in every finite stochastic moment. For linear equations, the reduction coincides with truncation of the first Wiener chaos. Lastly, as an application, we prove a high-probability local-in-time approximation theorem for stochastic Navier--Stokes equations, with finite measurements of both the initial condition and forcing and an explicit sensing rate.

summary_zh.method: 用Fourier截断把分布值噪声化为有限测量，结合Besov与Schauder估计构造ReLU分支-主干网络逼近解算子。

summary_en.result: Explicit bounds on the required number of forcing measurements and trunk functions are obtained in every finite stochastic moment, and a local-in-time approximation theorem is derived for stochastic Navier-Stokes equations.

papers.title: Cool Graphs: Active Property Search Towards Quantum Nano-Refrigerators
papers.abstract: Nanodevices that absorb energy from their thermal environment can act as quantum refrigerators. Finding suitable configurations, however, is a needle-in-a-haystack problem: the many-body state space scales exponentially with the size of the device, where each candidate configuration requires an expensive quantum-chemical computation. We introduce a search framework that couples a Graph Variational Autoencoder (GVAE) with an uncertainty-driven Active Learning (AL) loop to efficiently identify energy-absorbing configurations in electronic junctions with a 2D "working material" to be optimized. The GVAE maps physical parameters - site energies, coupling matrices, temperature - into a smooth latent space that distinguishes cooling from dissipative parameter regimes, achieving a classification discriminability of $0.920 \pm 0.004$ on held-out configurations and $0.895 \pm 0.010$ on unseen extrapolation topologies. An AL pipeline based on Monte Carlo dropout then targets the decision boundary, iteratively selecting the candidates where the model is least certain for simulation. Over 32 AL cycles, the uncertainty-driven strategy discovers energy absorbing systems at rates consistently exceeding the random baseline across all tested topologies (where only 1.9-8.4% of configurations exhibit the desired property), providing a data-efficient pathway for navigating a combinatorically large design space. The learned latent space organizes configurations along physically interpretable axes, that correlate with underlying microscopic model parameters. This hints at the existence of "cooling coordinates" - low-dimensional, physically interpretable quantities separating cooling from non-cooling regimes. Our framework, thus, paves a new way towards effective cooling of nanoscale electronic information processing devices, to reduce the environmental footprint of high performance computing.

papers.title: PrimeSim: A Generalist World Model Simulator from Large-Scale Cross-Embodiment Demonstrations
papers.abstract: A robot world model that serves as a simulator must do more than generate plausible videos: it must faithfully follow commanded actions, maintain consistency across camera views, and sustain coherent long-horizon rollouts. We present PrimeSim, an action-conditioned, multiview world model simulator that addresses these challenges through progressive midtraining and posttraining. Starting from a pretrained video generator, we midtrain on 30,110 hours of robot demonstrations spanning 22 platforms. To improve action following, we introduce a unified cross-embodiment action representation and frame-aligned dual-path conditioning to strengthen action-frame correspondence. To maintain multiview consistency, we develop view-aware interleaved attention with explicit camera identities, enabling cross-view information exchange while preserving view-specific representations. We further introduce a fast-video, slow-memory posttraining framework that transforms the bidirectional video generator into an efficient autoregressive simulator. By combining fast causal generation, self-rollout training, and hierarchical temporal memory, PrimeSim mitigates error accumulation from self-generated histories and supports coherent long-horizon simulation. PrimeSim runs at 10.1 FPS, remains stable over long-horizon rollouts on rigid and deformable manipulation tasks, and transfers to held-out platforms within 100 to 200 gradient steps where the pretrained backbone does not. Against five open-source action-conditioned world models it leads four of the five WorldSimProbe suites and posts the best overall EWMBench score, while fine-grained local calibration still trails the field; its rollouts are faithful enough to support GRPO-based policy optimization. We release the model weights, inference code, and training code.

papers.title: A Compact Residual-Screened Local Reduced-Order Model for Diffuse-Domain Shape Optimization
papers.abstract: We generalize the compact residual-screened local reduced-order model (CL-ROM) from Brinkman-penalized flow to shape optimization with the diffuse domain method (DDM). As with Brinkman penalization, DDM extends evolving-domain problems to a fixed rectangular domain, allowing one grid for discretization and directly compatible snapshots from different designs. Unlike Brinkman penalization, DDM uses a phase field to weight operators and sources and treats Dirichlet, Neumann and Robin conditions through diffuse boundary terms. The CL-ROM mechanism carries over: recent full-order and corrected solutions determine local reduced spaces, while residual screening, correction with retained factors and objective verification decide when a full-order solve is needed. We derive reduced operators, residuals and sensitivities for each diffuse model, using Galerkin projection for the symmetric problems and least-squares Petrov--Galerkin projection for nonlinear flow. For the symmetric problems we prove a local approximation estimate that admits inexact, corrected snapshots. In numerical tests of shape identification, drag minimization in Navier--Stokes channel flow and compliance minimization of a cantilever, CL-ROM uses reduced solutions for nearly all design updates, reproduces the full-order objectives with relative differences below $5\times10^{-6}$, and is $3.85$ to $7.65$ times faster than a full-order baseline that reuses factorizations as preconditioners.

papers.title: iMED: A Multi-Endoscope Dataset for Surgical 3D Perception
papers.abstract: We introduce iMED, the first synchronized multi-endoscope dataset for robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery (RAMIS), designed to address a fundamental limitation in surgical vision benchmarking: the absence of independent held-out viewpoints. Existing surgical datasets capture single-trajectory sequences from a single endoscope, making it impossible to distinguish geometric generalization from photometric interpolation along a narrow forward-facing path. iMED provides 340 sequences ~170K synchronized timepoints with 4 views per timepoint) recorded simultaneously from two independent stereo endoscopes across ex vivo, postmortem, and live surgical settings, spanning 14 specimens with diverse anatomical regions and motion regimes. The dataset includes calibrated camera intrinsics, ArUco-based frame-wise pose estimates with uncertainty quantification, instrument segmentation masks, and rich clinical metadata. Using a train-on-one-endoscope, test-on-another evaluation protocol, we benchmark 23 state-of-the-art methods across rigid and deformable novel view synthesis, pose estimation, feature matching, and monocular depth estimation. Our experiments show that methods relying primarily on photometric supervision degrade substantially under this held-out-endoscope setting, while methods with explicit geometric regularization are more robust across views in our benchmark. Notably, large-scale foundation models transfer surprisingly well to surgical imagery, often outperforming domain-specific models, suggesting pitfalls in current fine-tuning protocols. iMED establishes a new evaluation protocol for geometric generalization in surgical vision.

papers.title: Stabilizing Neural Emulation of Spatiotemporal Physical Dynamics through Denoising Koopman Latent Dynamics
papers.abstract: Koopman operator theory provides a principled framework for reduced-order modeling of nonlinear spatiotemporal dynamics through linear evolution in an observable space. In practice, however, learned finite-dimensional representations are typically approximately invariant, causing unresolved dynamics and accumulated closure errors. Recent approaches, inspired by the Mori-Zwanzig formalism, address these effects through deterministic memory or closure modeling, yet robust extrapolation beyond the training horizon remains challenging. Here, we propose KoopFlow, an efficient prediction-correction framework based on the key insight that finite-dimensional Koopman error accumulation can be reinterpreted as a progressive distributional degradation process. Accordingly, KoopFlow treats Koopman predictions as noisy intermediate estimates, which are then transported toward the target latent distribution through a generative model, thereby mitigating accumulated errors while retaining computational efficiency and temporal flexibility. Moreover, we reveal a non-monotonic relationship between Koopman spectral coherence and predictive accuracy. Experiments across diverse nonlinear dynamical systems demonstrate improved long-horizon prediction accuracy and stability over representative baselines, particularly beyond the training horizon.

papers.title: SCANO: Restoring Boundary-Condition Completeness in Sampled Meshes with a Sliced-Cross-Attention Neural Operator for 3D Thermal Fields
papers.abstract: Training neural operators on million-cell meshes can exceed GPU memory limits. Models are therefore trained on subsamples and deployed on whole meshes or selected regions. However, subsampling can distort boundary information, degrading accuracy. We ask when boundary conditioning under sampling stays consistent with whole-mesh training, and how to aggregate and inject boundary data. Representing the solution as an integral of boundary data against type-dependent measures, we show that subsampling distorts this conditioning in three ways: incomplete boundary coverage or a sample-dependent global state, face weighting by count rather than area, and compression of boundary inputs into a low-dimensional vector. This analysis yields four measurable consistency conditions checkable before training. We satisfy them with two backbone-agnostic modules. Boundary Quadrature Attention (BQA) aggregates all boundary faces, typed and area-weighted, into slice tokens that every query point reads at every layer. Anchored Global State (AGS) estimates the global state from anchors independent of the sampled points. Adding both to a scalable message-passing and slice-attention backbone yields SCANO. We evaluate the approach on controlled and public benchmarks and a data-centre thermal simulation dataset (DCTS) containing million-cell meshes. On both benchmarks, BQA improves every backbone, reducing whole-mesh error up to 15-fold. On all three datasets, AGS aligns regional with whole-mesh predictions, cutting regional error at least tenfold for most backbones on the public benchmark. Together, the modules nearly halve the best original backbone's whole-mesh error on both benchmarks. SCANO predicts a room-scale field in under one second, over 100 times faster than whole-room anchor self-attention.

papers.title: A research world model of power engineering learns its dynamics and reveals what-ifs
papers.abstract: Decisions about the direction of research in power engineering determine which technologies mature and, through them, shape infrastructure that lasts decades, yet their consequences cannot be observed before they are taken, and existing forecasts of research fields extrapolate a single trajectory. Here we introduce research world models, which treat a research field as a dynamical system that can be acted upon, and establish one for power engineering from 1.1 million papers. A distilled language model reads each paper into role-typed concepts, two sophisticated, high-fidelity graph-temporal neural network cores learn how the resulting concept network evolves, and operators learned from natural experiments in the publication record estimate the effects of interventions. In temporally held-out tests, the model forecast years ahead which concepts would grow and which method-target pairs would be joined for the first time, outperforming tuned machine-learning baselines in most settings, and its estimated intervention effects tracked those realized in natural experiments it had not seen. Its training scheme and three of its operators replicated in two fields withheld from development. Questions posed in natural language are compiled by a domain-specialized 27-billion-parameter language model into executable actions and answered as paired simulations with and without the intervention. The answers were rated 4.1 of 5 for faithfulness by an independent language-model judge. By revealing the latent dynamics of a research field and its response to interventions, research world models offer a new way to simulate and test research decisions before they are made.

papers.title: Hybrid Particle-Voxel Dynamics for Multimodal 3D World Simulation
papers.abstract: Predicting how the world evolves in response to robot actions is central to policy learning, evaluation, and planning. However, many action-conditioned world models predict future observations in 2D image or video space without explicitly modeling the underlying 3D scene, making spatial consistency across viewpoints and over long-horizon interactions challenging. We introduce 3D World Simulator, an action-conditioned multimodal world modeling framework that jointly predicts appearance, geometry, and tactile observations from a unified 3D representation. Our approach combines a hybrid particle-voxel autoencoder that compresses point clouds into compact 3D voxel latents with an action-conditioned latent dynamics model that predicts their evolution. The shared 3D representation supports geometrically consistent rendering from arbitrary viewpoints and flexible integration of spatially aligned tactile signals. Our experiments demonstrate interactive, long-horizon, multimodal prediction at 50 Hz. We then show how our model enables scalable data generation for policy training and evaluation using tactile and multi-view visual observations, including wrist-mounted and novel camera views. Furthermore, we scale our method to large datasets containing diverse objects and demonstrate model-based planning with unseen objects and robot configurations. Together, these results highlight the potential of hybrid particle-voxel dynamics as a foundation for multimodal 3D world simulation.

papers.title: Integrating Machine Learning and Uncertainty Quantification for Real-Time Decision-Making in Digital Twins: A System-Centric Review and Perspective
papers.abstract: Digital Twins are evolving from passive virtual representations into closed-loop systems that continuously synchronize with physical assets and drive real-time decisions. Yet predictive modeling, machine learning (ML), uncertainty quantification (UQ), and decision-making have been studied as separate capabilities, leaving limited understanding of their integration and maintenance during online operation. This narrative review, scoped by the functional requirements of real-time decision-making rather than by Digital Twin terminology alone, examines how such decisions are generated and sustained in engineering Digital Twins. We first examine foundational decision-making architectures and representative engineering applications, followed by methods that address their limitations across the decision loop. We identify optimization-based, policy-based, and knowledge-based approaches as the major pathways from virtual representation to action. Across them, ML plays three roles in decision-making: enabling efficient surrogate modeling, transforming heterogeneous physical feedback into decision-relevant information, and accelerating or directly generating decisions. UQ supports uncertainty-aware decisions and model adaptation, while continual validation, drift detection, and adaptation help maintain reliable operation as the physical system evolves. Together, these findings underscore the need for a shift from a model-centric to a system-centric perspective on Digital Twins, where its performance depends on the interactions with sensing, state estimation, computation, decision-making, and adaptation rather than on their standalone performance. Therefore, future research should shift from isolated algorithm development toward system-level co-design, scalable decision-making, and approaches to design, and data-efficient continual adaptation and validation for AI-enabled autonomous systems.

papers.title: ActOR: Ambient AI-Based Agentic Orchestration for Humanoid Autonomy in Operating Rooms
papers.abstract: Operating rooms (ORs) increasingly contain ambient sensing infrastructure to enable AI-based optimization of workflows and utilization. We pursue an alternative path: using ambient AI to guide robot action and optimize utilization. Deploying humanoids in the OR without ambient AI is severely limited by cumbersome de novo orientation and planning due to partial onboard observations. We posit that this can be achieved by coupling an ambient AI-based agentic orchestrator with the humanoid robotic actor, providing shared perception and execution feedback for humanoid autonomy in the OR. ActOR fuses a wall-mounted ambient camera and the robot's head-mounted camera into a shared object-level digital twin (DT). A large language model agent plans over the DT using pre-programmed locomotion and manipulation skills without task-specific training. During execution, DT updates and execution outcomes inform retries, alternative approaches, or replanning. We evaluated ActOR in simulated and physical environments. Across three tasks in two simulated ORs reconstructed from real rooms, ambient perception reduced exploration from 1.05 to 0.12 Explore calls per trial when targets were initially outside the robot's view. Closed-loop feedback increased success from 46.7% to 83.3% under nominal execution and from 8.3% to 51.7% under injected navigation, object-relocation, and grasp perturbations. In a physical mock OR with a humanoid, ActOR completed 14 of 20 single-object disposal trials and demonstrated replanning after scene changes. Ambient AI-based observations provide scene state that improves robot action planning, increasing success and reducing exploration compared with robot-only observations. Feeding skill outcomes and DT updates back to the planner improves multi-step task success. Our results show the feasibility of humanoid task autonomy for multi-step disposal tasks in a mock OR.

papers.title: Constructing a Regional Slang Lexicon for Electricity Demands via Soft-Label Bidirectional Anchoring and Active Learning
papers.abstract: Power-grid customer service increasingly relies on community social media, where customers describe outages, billing, and equipment faults in informal regional dialect. Such messages exhibit non-standard morphology, semantic drift, and out-of-vocabulary expressions that make manual lexicon construction costly and degrade conventional NLP tools. We propose a weak-supervision framework constructing a regional slang lexicon from curated dialect anchors and power-domain seed terms. Candidates are generated via Pointwise Mutual Information with soft-label bidirectional anchoring, retaining dialect-anchored terms while recording power-domain relevance as separate metadata, and are scored by combining Sentence-BERT semantic similarity with a jieba-based wordhood measure. Uncertainty-aware active learning with rule-based and retrieval-augmented LLM oracles is applied under three query strategies, and the resulting lexicon is evaluated by a higher-capability LLM calibrated against human expert annotations via Cohen's $κ$. On 11,177 real WeChat messages from Yuxi (Yunnan, China), the framework achieves an evaluator-estimated dialect precision of DP~$=$~1.0 with zero false positives. An ablation shows that soft-label layering retains 751\% more candidates than strict power-gating at identical precision, expanding the candidate pool from 41 to 349 terms. Human calibration ($n=46$) yields $κ_{\text{dialect}}=1.0$ and $κ_{\text{power}}=0.85$. The resulting 25--33-term lexicon, 4--5 of which are power-relevant, provides a preliminary resource for dialect-aware power-grid service NLP.

papers.title: CT-based navigation for acetabular cup placement in supine and lateral positions: a simulated surgery study using patient-specific 3D-printed pelvic models
papers.abstract: Purpose Accurate acetabular cup placement is critical for the success of total hip arthroplasty (THA). The aim of this study was to evaluate the accuracy and precision of a CT-based, AI-driven navigation tool for acetabular cup placement in supine and lateral patient positions, using a patient-specific 3D-printed pelvic model with an embedded acetabular cup rim as a physical measurement reference. Methods Twenty-six patient-specific pelvic models were generated from preoperative CT data. A virtual acetabular cup was added to each pelvic mesh, cropped to the rim, and 3D-printed together with the bone, yielding a physical cup reference embedded in the printed pelvis. The ground-truth cup orientation and position were defined within the planning application by overlaying a cup component template on the embedded rim. Each model was tested once in supine and once in lateral position in a paired design. Ten cases were repeated three times per position to assess intra-session precision. Outcomes were surface matching root-mean-square error (RMSE), cup anteversion, inclination, and depth errors. Analyses included two one-sided tests (TOST) for equivalence (±0.5 mm), Bland–Altman agreement, Levene's test, and intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC). Results Mean alignment-point RMSE was 0.26 mm (supine) and 0.28 mm (lateral); mean independent test-point RMSE was 0.30 mm in both positions, with TOST confirming equivalence within ±0.5 mm. Mean absolute anteversion error was 0.67° (supine) and 0.44° (lateral), with comparable inclination errors. Mean absolute cup depth error remained well below ±3 mm. Bland–Altman analyses showed narrow 95% limits of agreement between positions. All ICC(3,1) values for cup orientation exceeded 0.99 in both positions. Conclusions The evaluated navigation tool achieved sub-millimeter surface matching, small cup placement errors, and excellent intra-session precision in both supine and lateral positions. The embedded-rim phantom enabled direct measurement of cup orientation and seating depth on the printed model and is applicable to other CT-based navigation systems.

papers.title: Influence of Implant Macrodesign on Primary Stability Across Different Bone Density Models: A Comparative In Vitro Study
papers.abstract: Background: Implant macrogeometry and bone density are major determinants of primary stability. This study aimed to evaluate primary stability across different implant macrodesigns and block models. Materials and Methods: A total of 153 implants were divided into Group 1 (AnyRidge), Group 2 (BlueDiamond RC), and Group 3 (BlueDiamond NC) (n = 51 each). Each implant was sequentially tested in synthetic D1–D4 bone models. Insertion torque values (ITV) and implant stability quotient (ISQ) were recorded. Results: In D1, ITV was highest in Group 1 (69.51 ± 1.50 Ncm), followed by Group 2 (53.82 ± 6.75 Ncm) and Group 3 (49.31 ± 7.00 Ncm) (p < 0.01, p < 0.001). In D4, ITV decreased to 34.71 ± 3.23, 19.90 ± 3.08, and 11.18 ± 2.14 Ncm, respectively (p < 0.001). D1 ISQ values were 84.53 ± 2.51, 72.08 ± 3.69, and 66.33 ± 2.63, respectively (p < 0.001). In D4, ISQ values were 60.29 ± 3.84, 52.86 ± 3.73, and 52.18 ± 2.48, respectively (p < 0.001); Groups 2 and 3 did not differ significantly. Conclusions: Implant macrodesign influences primary stability, with AnyRidge demonstrating the highest ITV and ISQ values in D1 as well as D4. Further clinical studies would be beneficial to support these findings.

papers.title: Axial Compression Properties of a Novel Octopus‐Inspired Lattice Structure
papers.abstract: Lattice structures are widely valued for high energy absorption (EA) efficiency and lightweight features. To further improve the EA efficiency and deformation stability, this study proposes a novel biomimetic octopus lattice structure (OLS) inspired by the unique claw morphology of octopuses. The OLS sample was fabricated using selective laser sintering, and axial compression experiments were performed to validate the accuracy of finite element analysis (FEA). OLS exhibits superior EA capability through the unique fence‐type deformation pattern. To systematically explore its mechanical potential, the influence of key geometric parameters on the compression performance of OLS was investigated. Results demonstrate that EA is significantly enhanced with increased wall thickness. Specifically, the specific energy absorption (SEA) value of an OLS with 1.0 mm thickness is 79.82% higher than that with 0.6 mm. The layer number critically influences performance, with the six‐layer OLS increasing SEA by 193.81% compared with the two‐layer OLS. The two‐layer OLS exhibits a lantern‐type deformation pattern. In summary, the OLS demonstrates remarkable EA properties and a unique deformation pattern, offering innovative insights for the design of high‐efficiency EA devices.

papers.title: Cost-Effective Engineering Strategies to Improve 3D Bioprinting: Practical Modifications and Smart Technological Horizons
papers.abstract: 3D bioprinting has evolved from developing simple cellular constructs to fabricating intricate, physiologically relevant tissue models. However, translation is bottlenecked by high equipment costs and processing trade-offs. This narrative review evaluates cost-effective engineering strategies over the past five years designed to enhance printing fidelity independently of material-chemistry innovations. Our observation reveals that thermal stabilization (2–60 °C) and static mixing elements yield resolutions down to 15 µm from cell-friendly 1 mm nozzles, while automated nozzle arrays accelerate spheroid processing 10 times. In-flow microfluidic gelation and self-healing granular baths eliminate architectural collapse, successfully preserving blood-vessel lumens (~50 µm). Additionally, newly developed procedural strategies significantly optimize output: nozzle-free painting and delayed-mixing droplet collision bypass clogging limits to handle ultra-dense networks, while vat-free projection methods reduce bioink waste to under 1%. These affordable modifications consistently preserve high post-printing cell viability (>90%) across complex, heterogeneous configurations. Ultimately, we conclude that the future of biofabrication relies on a transition toward closed-loop, AI-driven parameter optimization and the systematic integration of bioprinting platforms with active bioreactors to guide early structural constructs into functional, mature tissues.

papers.title: Temperature-dependent tribological performance of HVOF-thermal sprayed FeCoCrNiAl HEA coating deposited on TC4 alloy
papers.abstract: Abstract A FeCoCrNiAl high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating was deposited on a Ti-6Al-4V (TC4) alloy substrate by high-velocity oxygen fuel (HVOF) thermal spraying to enhance its sliding wear performance. Reciprocating sliding tests were conducted from 25 to 300 °C, and the temperature-dependent friction behavior, wear morphology, and damage evolution were examined. Meanwhile, an Archard-based finite element model incorporating the arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian adaptive mesh technique was established to reproduce the progressive wear process. The coating exhibited a compact lamellar microstructure, a BCC-dominated phase constitution, and higher hardness than the TC4 substrate. Although friction and wear increased with temperature for both materials, the coated specimens consistently showed lower coefficients of friction and less severe surface damage. Compared with the TC4 substrate, the HEA coating reduced the maximum wear depth and wear volume by 30.7% and 23.7%, respectively, at 25 °C, while the corresponding reductions reached 41.2% and 40.8% at 300 °C. Notably, the maximum reductions of 49.3% and 42.4%, respectively, were obtained at 200 °C, demonstrating that the protective effect of the coating became more pronounced at elevated temperatures. The wear of TC4 evolved from ploughing and plastic deformation to oxidation-assisted fatigue damage, whereas the coating mainly underwent mild abrasion, oxidation, and localized inter-splat delamination. The simulated wear profiles agreed well with the experimental results, with deviations below 5%, and revealed a reduced stress concentration in the coated specimens. These findings demonstrate that HVOF-sprayed FeCoCrNiAl coatings can effectively suppress temperature-induced wear degradation of TC4 alloy.

papers.title: Cranioplasty in the 21st Century: Bridging Neurosurgery, Biomaterials, and Regenerative Frontiers
papers.abstract: Abstract Cranioplasty restores skull integrity following trauma, decompression, tumor removal, or congenital deformity. Choosing the right implant material is crucial for structural protection and aesthetic durability. Available materials include autologous bone, metals, polymers, and composites—each with distinct advantages and limitations. Advances in materials science and manufacturing have introduced technologies such as patient-specific 3D printed implants, bioactive ceramics, and regenerative scaffolds. A narrative review of studies published between 2005–2025 on PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science identified studies on “cranioplasty,” “biomaterials,” and materials such as polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA), titanium, and polyetheretherketone (PEEK). Data on biomechanics, biological response, infection, failure, imaging compatibility, cost, and usability were extracted. Current cranioplasty practice relies on few established materials. Autologous bone provides perfect anatomical match but risks resorption and infection, especially in children. PMMA is inexpensive, rigid, and radiolucent but brittle and biologically inert. Titanium offers strength and low infection rates but is costly and unsuitable for growing skulls. PEEK closely mimics bone elasticity and imaging transparency, giving excellent aesthetics but high expense and poor osseointegration. Emerging solutions, such as 3D printing, hydroxyapatite (HA) ceramics, and regenerative constructs, aim to improve integration and reduce complications. There is no universal ideal material. Selection should depend on patient age, defect characteristics, infection, and resources. While autologous bone remains preferred when feasible, PMMA, titanium, and PEEK each offer advantages. Ongoing development of bioactive and regenerative implants represents the future of personalized cranial reconstruction.

papers.title: Three-dimensional alveolar ridge augmentation combined with photobiomodulation therapy for post-traumatic bone loss: clinical protocol, case report, and evidence review
papers.abstract: Post-traumatic alveolar ridge deficiencies often involve three-dimensional bone loss, making dental implant placement highly challenging. Guided bone regeneration techniques, combined with fixation devices, soft tissue substitutes, and adjunctive photobiomodulation therapy, have been proposed to enhance predictability and clinical outcomes. A 46-year-old female with severe alveolar bone loss, insufficient keratinized tissue, and maxillary sinus pneumatization following trauma was treated. Simultaneous three-dimensional ridge augmentation was performed using cortical cancellous Regen Allograft stabilized with bone plates and tenting screws. An open sinus lift was carried out with graft placement beneath the elevated Schneiderian membrane and coverage with a collagen membrane. Soft tissue management included palatal tissue mobilization and placement of acellular dermal matrix (Regen Allograft) under the flap. Postoperative photobiomodulation therapy was applied using an 808 nm diode laser (0.2 W, 4 J/cm²) to enhance soft and hard tissue healing. After six months of healing, six implants (IRES, volution, SVB) were placed under guided surgery, followed by screw-retained prosthetic rehabilitation. Clinical and CBCT examinations were performed during a 24-month follow-up period. CBCT evaluation at six months demonstrated sufficient horizontal and vertical bone regeneration, enabling successful placement of six implants with satisfactory primary stability. Soft tissue healing progressed uneventfully, with favorable tissue maturation and minimal postoperative discomfort. Prosthetic rehabilitation was completed successfully, and clinical and radiographic follow-up over 24 months revealed stable peri-implant bone levels, healthy peri implant soft tissues, satisfactory esthetic and functional outcomes, and no biological or mechanical complications. This case demonstrates that combining bone grafting with fixation devices, sinus augmentation, acellular dermal matrix, and photobiomodulation can successfully manage complex post-traumatic ridge deficiencies. The multidisciplinary approach provided predictable functional and esthetic outcomes.

papers.title: Propolis-loaded 3D bioprinted alginate/poly(vinyl)alcohol constructs for healing of full thickness skin wounds
papers.abstract: Objectives The development of bioactive wound dressings capable of actively modulating the healing microenvironment remains a critical challenge in regenerative medicine. In this study, a hybrid alginate/poly(vinyl alcohol) (Alg/PVA) hydrogel scaffold was fabricated by 3D bioprinting and subsequently functionalized with propolis to obtain a structurally stable and biologically active wound dressing. Methods A hybrid Alg/PVA hydrogel scaffold was fabricated using 3D bioprinting. Propolis loading was performed to introduce multifunctional biological activities, which were systematically evaluated via physicochemical characterization, surface hydrophilicity, water absorption, and propolis release kinetics. Antioxidant activity, antibacterial efficacy against S. aureus and E. coli , and fibroblast adhesion, proliferation, and migration were also assessed. Finally, in vivo wound healing studies were conducted over 21 days in a rat model. Results The incorporation of PVA improved the printability, mechanical integrity, and degradation behavior of the alginate-based scaffold, while propolis provided multifunctional biological activity. Propolis-loaded scaffolds exhibited enhanced surface hydrophilicity, controlled water absorption, and suitable water vapor transmission rates. Sustained propolis release provided antioxidant activity and inhibited the growth of both S. aureus and E. coli . In addition, the propolis-functionalized scaffolds supported fibroblast adhesion, proliferation, and migration. Wound healing studies showed accelerated wound closure, enhanced collagen deposition, and improved angiogenesis over 21 days for propolis-loaded scaffolds relative to non-loaded Alg/PVA scaffolds. Conclusions These results demonstrate that 3D bioprinted propolis-functionalized Alg/PVA scaffolds represent a promising multifunctional platform for wound healing.

papers.title: Intelligent bioprinting of biomimetic hemostatic constructs: From bioink design and programmable fabrication to preclinical validation for non-compressible hemorrhage
papers.abstract: Non-compressible hemorrhage (NCH) remains a leading cause of preventable trauma mortality because conventional gauze and oxidized cellulose act as passive barriers, whereas fibrin sealants depend on patient-derived fibrinogen; neither is reliable in coagulopathic patients. Recent convergence of bioink engineering, 3D/4D bioprinting, and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted material design enables the fabrication of biomimetic hemostatic constructs with programmable composition, multiscale architecture, and dynamic responsiveness. This review critically examines how intelligent bioprinting—integrating stimuli-responsive bioinks, multi-axis extrusion/digital light processing printing, and AI-guided bioink optimization—fundamentally differs from conventional biomaterial fabrication in recapitulating the structural mechanics of natural thrombi. We first analyze the structure–function relationships of native fibrin/platelet/red blood cell networks that should be mimicked by bioprinted constructs. We then systematically compare bioink formulations (natural biopolymers, synthetic peptides, cell-membrane-coated nano-vectors, and inorganic–organic composites) across four bioprinting-relevant dimensions: printability, post-printing bioactivity, wet-tissue adhesion strength, and burst pressure. We further evaluate cross-tier preclinical validation, including microfluidic thrombosis-on-chip, small-animal models, and lethal large-animal NCH models (porcine liver/spleen/junctional injury), with explicit differentiation from rodent wound-healing studies. Finally, we identify translational bottlenecks (rheological paradox, Good Manufacturing Practice scale-up, regulatory pathways) and articulate future directions: AI-guided bioink discovery, organ-on-chip patient-specific screening, and deployable 4D-printed hemostats. By bridging biomimetic design, programmable fabrication, and quantitative translational evaluation, intelligent bioprinting offers a manufacturable and clinically translatable route to next-generation NCH therapeutics.

papers.title: Patient- Surgery-and Implant-Related Predictors of Complications, Reoperation and Implant Survivorship Following Revision Total Hip Arthroplasty: A Longitudinal Cohort Study
papers.abstract: Background: Revision total hip arthroplasty is technically demanding and is associated with higher risks of complications, reoperation and implant failure than primary arthroplasty. Outcomes may be influenced by patient characteristics, surgical complexity and implant-related factors. Identification of these predictors may support risk stratification, perioperative optimization and improved surgical planning. Aim: To evaluate patient-, surgery- and implant-related predictors of complications, reoperation and implant survivorship following revision total hip arthroplasty. Materials and Methods: This longitudinal cohort study included 140 adult patients who underwent revision total hip arthroplasty at a tertiary care hospital. Patient-related variables, indication for revision, operative characteristics, bone loss, fixation method, bearing surface and implant-related factors were recorded. Patients were followed for postoperative complications, reoperations and implant failure. Predictors of complications and reoperation were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression. Implant survivorship was estimated using KaplanMeier analysis, and independent predictors of failure were determined using Cox proportional-hazards regression. A p value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results: The mean age was 66.8±10.9 years, and 59.3% of patients were male. Aseptic loosening was the most frequent indication for revision (33.6%), followed by periprosthetic joint infection (22.1%). Postoperative complications occurred in 43 (30.7%; 95% CI: 23.7-38.8) patients, while 24 (17.1%; 95% CI: 11.8-24.2) underwent reoperation. Dislocation was the most common complication (9.3%). Implant failure requiring repeat revision or component removal occurred in 17 (12.1%) patients. Advanced age, obesity, ASA class III-IV, infection-related revision, severe bone loss, operative duration >180 minutes, blood loss >1000 mL and component malposition independently predicted complications. Significant predictors of reoperation included age ≥70 years, two or more previous revisions, revision for infection and component malposition. Implant survivorship was 97.1% at six months, 94.2% at one year, 90.2% at two years and 85.9% at three years. Revision for periprosthetic joint infection (aHR=3.12; 95% CI: 1.18-8.26; p=0.022), Paprosky type III-IV bone loss (aHR=2.73; 95% CI: 1.04-7.17; p=0.042) and postoperative component malposition (aHR=2.86; 95% CI: 1.05-7.79; p=0.039) independently predicted implant failure. Conclusion: Complications and reoperations were relatively common following revision total hip arthroplasty, and implant survivorship declined progressively during follow-up. Infection-related revision, severe bone loss and component malposition were the principal independent predictors of implant failure. Improved infection control, reconstruction of bone defects and accurate component positioning may improve outcomes and implant longevity.

papers.title: Regenerative Surface Engineering of Dental Implants: Biological Strategies and Translational Perspectives
papers.abstract: Improvements in early biological responses to engineered dental implant surfaces have not consistently translated into superior long-term survival, marginal bone stability, or prevention of peri-implant disease relative to contemporary surfaces. This narrative review focuses on titanium implants and abutments, examining six complementary strategies: osseointegration, soft-tissue integration, antibacterial activity, osteoimmunomodulation, periodontal ligament regeneration, and multifunctional and smart surfaces. It evaluates their biological rationale alongside the preclinical and clinical evidence supporting their use. Experimental studies demonstrate changes in cell attachment, bone formation, microbial control, and immune regulation, while responsive systems coordinate these functions through controlled release or activation. Most emerging approaches remain supported predominantly by preclinical evidence. Future development should match surface functions to the requirements of each implant region and healing stage. Clinical translation requires reproducible performance and comparative studies demonstrating benefits in patient-relevant outcomes, including loading safety, tissue stability, and long-term maintainability.

papers.title: Deep Wavelet Diffeomorphism: A New Approach to Manifold Reshaping for PINN Training
papers.abstract: Abstract Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) are a mesh-free, data-driven approach for solving partial differential equations (PDEs). However, their accuracy in capturing strong-gradient regions (such as shock waves) depends on dense, uniform collocation points, which can lead to convergence issues and susceptibility to local optima. Traditional adaptive wavelet solvers excel at identifying discontinuous regions but suffer from time-step constraints and require cumbersome threshold tuning. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a Deep Wavelet Diffeomorphism (DWD) framework that integrates the strengths of both methods through a decoupled mechanism involving manifold regularization and low-dimensional training. Leveraging interpolating multiresolution analysis, DWD constructs a deep wavelet diffeomorphism that maps distorted physical-space training manifolds into smooth computational-space manifolds, while generating an optimal non-uniform collocation set---dense in feature-rich regions and sparse in smooth regions. This manifold mapping discretizes high-dimensional PDEs into a low-dimensional collocation system, which is then input into a standard PINN for efficient and stable optimization. Experimental results demonstrate that DWD achieves accuracy comparable to uniform super-resolution PINNs, while reducing collocation points by an order of magnitude and shortening training time by 5 to 8 times. It outperforms pure wavelet solvers and traditional PINNs in both accuracy and robustness. Concise and compatible with existing deep learning pipelines, DWD offers a data-efficient, low-dimensional discretization approach for high-dimensional PDEs and inverse problems in physics-informed learning.

papers.title: Global sensitivity analysis for stochastic models of infectious diseases: Re-emergence of yellow fever virus in the Americas as a case study
papers.abstract: Abstract Emerging infectious diseases are a persistent public health threat that challenge deterministic, mechanistic modeling approaches. Because outbreaks initially start with a low number of infected hosts, their dynamics are highly stochastic, making traditional deterministic methods, e.g. ordinary differential equations, unable to qualitatively or quantitatively capture the transmission dynamics. In place, stochastic models are used, such as Markov chain models, but these models present their own challenges. Often, to infer a quantity of interest with stochastic models, we need to sample the model’s distribution many times over, introducing an additional source of noise to our analysis. This additional noise makes the inference of our quantity of interest more difficult and computationally expensive. Here, we show how novel tools from the field of uncertainty quantification can be used to efficiently separate these two channels of noise, allowing us to make rigorous statistical inferences about processes important for disease emergence. We illustrate these techniques with a model of yellow fever virus spillover in the Americas, a virus that has seen rapid re-emergence amongst multiple hosts and vectors in South America over the last decade. We show that only a handful of parameters’ uncertainties greatly affect variation in cumulative disease incidence. In particular, uncertainty in patch connectivity and non-human primate latency has the greatest impact on the variation of cumulative disease incidence of yellow fever virus across patches. Author Contributions Conceptualization: Nate Kornetzke, Helen J. Wearing. Methodology: Nate Kornetzke, Helen J. Wearing. Formal Analysis: Nate Kornetzke. Software: Nate Kornetzke. Visualization: Nate Kornetzke. Writing, Original Draft Preparation: Nate Kornetzke. Writing, Review and Editing: Helen J. Wearing. Supervision: Helen J. Wearing. Author Summary Emerging infectious diseases are a growing threat to public health. Computational models allow researchers to forecast future disease burdens and to investigate counterfactual scenarios, and often, these models are stochastic, i.e. contain randomness, to capture the qualitative behavior of emergence. A type of statistical analysis known as global sensitivity analysis allows modelers to rigorously analyze how varying the input to a model affects variation in its outputs. This type of analysis helps us infer what mechanisms are important for disease mitigation and control, especially when an infectious disease has a complex ecology consisting of multiple hosts and vectors. Until recently, stochastic models of emerging infectious diseases often proved too computationally expensive to perform a global sensitivity analysis on. Here, we demonstrate how new mathematical tools allow us to streamline this process for complex models of emerging infectious diseases. We analyze the ecology of re-emerging yellow fever in South America, a public health threat occurring in many hosts and vectors across vastly different ecosystems.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: A Statistical Perspective
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has emerged as a central framework for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences. Despite its practical success, RLHF raises fundamental statistical questions because it relies on noisy, subjective, and heterogeneous feedback to learn reward models and optimize policies. This review provides a statistical perspective on RLHF, focusing primarily on LLM alignment. We introduce the main components of RLHF, including supervised fine-tuning, reward modeling, and policy optimization, and relate them to familiar statistical concepts such as the Bradley–Terry–Luce model, latent utility estimation, active learning, experimental design, and uncertainty quantification. We review methods for learning reward functions from pairwise preference data and for optimizing policies through both two-stage RLHF pipelines and emerging one-stage approaches such as direct preference optimization. We further discuss recent extensions including reinforcement learning from artificial intelligence feedback, inference-time algorithms, and reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, as well as benchmark datasets, evaluation protocols, and open-source frameworks that support RLHF research. We conclude by highlighting open challenges in RLHF.

papers.title: Constructivist learning, control-value appraisals and achievement emotions in further education mathematics: a mixed methods study on the determinants of enjoyment and anxiety
papers.abstract: Enjoyment and anxiety towards learning mathematics can significantly impact learning and achievement. Within the theoretical framework of the control-value theory (CVT) of achievement emotions, the current research explored the role of perceived cognitive constructivist principles in Further Education (FE) mathematics classrooms as antecedents of these emotions for adult students, among whom negative beliefs and emotions towards mathematics are prevalent. This mixed methods research comprised two sequential studies. First, a quantitative, questionnaire-based study with a correlational design identified the extent to which perceptions of constructivist learning, control-value appraisals, enjoyment and anxiety were related using a sample of adult students (N = 103) of mathematics in FE. Next, one-to-one interviews with seven students and six teachers in FE sought to explain the quantitative results and explore the underlying conditions that determine the effectiveness of constructivist learning practices in creating positive emotional expereinces in FE mathematics. Consolidation of findings across the two studies suggest that cognitive-constructivist informed practices such as active learning and contextualised tasks may elicit enjoyment and reduce anxiety towards mathematical content via shaping positive appraisals of control and value, whereas a social learning environment is conducive to creating overall positive learning experiences for these students. Implications for practice are discussed.

papers.title: Simulation-based ward rounds in preclinical medical education: a case study in medical parasitology
papers.abstract: Preclinical medical education must help students connect foundational knowledge with clinical contexts, yet opportunities for clinically contextualized active learning remain limited in discipline-specific courses such as Medical Parasitology. Simulation-based ward rounds (SBWR) may provide such an opportunity, but evidence regarding their implementation and student experience in preclinical medical education is limited. We conducted a post-intervention mixed-methods educational evaluation of SBWR embedded in the discussion component of a compulsory Medical Parasitology course for third-year medical students from five-year Clinical Medicine, five-year Stomatology, Anesthesiology, and Preventive Medicine. Each group contained approximately 10–15 students and completed one 45-minute SBWR session during the same teaching week. Across 10 parallel groups, 139 students participated in SBWR, of whom 92 voluntarily completed the post-session questionnaire. Respondents were categorized into a role-playing group ( n = 49) and a non-role-playing group ( n = 43) according to whether they assumed an active scenario role. Quantitative responses were summarized descriptively and exploratory between-group comparisons were performed. Open-ended responses were coded inductively to identify recurring implementation themes. Students reported high overall satisfaction with SBWR (mean 8.84 ± 1.13 on a 10-point scale). Across questionnaire items, the role-playing group gave descriptively higher ratings on several learning-related items, but no between-group difference reached statistical significance. For the clinical reasoning item, 63.3% of students in the role-playing group selected the highest rating, compared with 48.8% in the non-role-playing group. However, the difference did not reach statistical significance. Open-ended feedback identified unclear procedures, insufficient role preparation or organization, limited case information, and scenario setup as areas for improvement. Students reported favorable experiences with SBWR as a clinically contextualized learning activity in preclinical medical education. Because the study used a post-intervention self-report design without a non-SBWR control group or objective learning assessment, the findings should be interpreted as evidence of acceptability and perceived learning experience rather than educational effectiveness. Controlled studies incorporating objective outcomes are needed.

papers.title: A generalized model predictive fault-tolerant control strategy for hybrid multilevel converter under arbitrary open-circuit failures
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the fault-tolerant (FT) operation of the T-type converter using a cascaded H-bridge (T 2 C-HB) topology under open-circuit failures (OCF) occurring in any IGBT switch. The high number of switches in the hybrid multilevel converter (HMC) increases the possibility of switch faults. However, existing FT control methods for HMC primarily focus on local faults, making them ineffective in addressing global faults and thereby limiting overall system reliability. To achieve global FT control, this paper proposes an FT strategy based on model predictive control (FT-MPC), which consists of two stages. In the first stage, the optimal redundant voltage vector position is determined by employing an optimal current tracking strategy. In the second stage, an initialization function is introduced to integrate various types of OCF into a unified framework. By employing weighting factors within the selected redundant voltage vectors, the optimal switching states are determined. The proposed method effectively handles various types of OCF and is applicable to any HMC incorporating cascaded H-bridge modules. Simulation and experimental results validate the feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed method.
